subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: 5.5 Rotational Equilibrium and Newton’s First Law in Rotational Form
5.6 Newton’s Second Law in Rotational Form

questions.q: A rigid wheel rotates about a fixed axle through its center. Which statement about the motion of the wheel's points is correct?
options: At each instant, every point of the wheel moves in the same direction, as the wheel is rigid.
At each instant, points at opposite ends of a diameter move in opposite directions.
In each second, points near the axle turn through a larger angle than points near the rim.
Modeling the wheel as one object at its center describes how each of its points moves.
optionWhy: A student who thinks 'rigid' means that all the points move together picks this. That is true only for a rigid system that translates without rotating; in rotation, each point's velocity is tangent to its own circle, so points in different places move in different directions.

The wheel keeps its shape, but each point moves along its own circle around the axle. Two points at opposite ends of a diameter therefore have velocities in opposite directions at every instant. This is why a rigid system cannot be modeled as a single object when its rotation is described.

A student who thinks a point on a smaller circle gets around it sooner picks this. All points of a rigid wheel turn through the same angle in the same time; points near the rim travel along longer arcs, not through larger angles.

A student who applies the object model to a rotating system picks this. A single object at the center of a wheel spinning on a fixed axle would not move at all, while the wheel's points do; describing the rotation needs angular quantities.
questions.explain: The wheel keeps its shape, but each point moves along its own circle around the axle. Two points at opposite ends of a diameter therefore have velocities in opposite directions at every instant. This is why a rigid system cannot be modeled as a single object when its rotation is described.

questions.q: A baton is tossed into the air and spins end over end as it flies. Air resistance is negligible. Which statement about modeling the baton is correct?
options: It can be modeled as one object to find the greatest height reached by its center of mass.
It cannot be modeled as one object for any part of its motion, because it is spinning.
It can be modeled as one object to find the path of each of its ends, as it is rigid.
It can be modeled as one object to find how fast it spins, from the speed of its center.
optionWhy: The center of mass moves like a single object in free fall whatever the spin, so the greatest height it reaches can be found with the object model. The spin does not affect the motion of the center of mass, so it can be ignored for this question.

A student who thinks any rotation rules out the object model picks this. A rotating system can be treated as one object for any motion that its center of mass describes, such as the height that the baton's center reaches.

A student who thinks every point of a rigid system moves the same way picks this. The ends of the spinning baton loop around its center of mass, so their paths differ from the center's parabola and cannot be found from the object model.

A student who links the spin to the speed of the center of mass picks this. The two motions are independent: the same toss could send the baton up spinning fast or slowly, and a single object at the center of mass carries no information about rotation.
questions.explain: The center of mass moves like a single object in free fall whatever the spin, so the greatest height it reaches can be found with the object model. The spin does not affect the motion of the center of mass, so it can be ignored for this question.

questions.q: A disk can rotate about a fixed axle, with counterclockwise taken as positive. A mark on the disk starts at angular position θ₀ = 0.400 rad. The disk turns 1.50 revolutions counterclockwise and then 0.250 revolution clockwise. What is the disk's angular displacement?
options: 11.0 rad
8.25 rad
1.57 rad
7.85 rad
optionWhy: A student who adds the two turns as if both were in the same sense picks this: 1.75 rev × 2π rad = 11.0 rad, the total angle turned. The clockwise turn is in the negative sense, so it reduces the angular displacement.

A student who gives the final angular position as the displacement picks this: 0.400 rad + 7.85 rad = 8.25 rad. Angular displacement is the change θ − θ₀, so the starting value is subtracted again, leaving 7.85 rad.

A student who thinks a whole revolution adds nothing, because the mark is back where it started, keeps only the extra quarter turn: 0.25 × 2π rad = 1.57 rad. Angular position keeps counting through full turns, so the whole revolution adds 2π rad.
Give each turn its sign: +1.50 rev − 0.250 rev = +1.25 rev. Converting, Δθ = 1.25 × 2π rad = 7.85 rad. The starting position does not matter, because Δθ = θ − θ₀ is a change in angular position.
questions.explain: Give each turn its sign: +1.50 rev − 0.250 rev = +1.25 rev. Converting, Δθ = 1.25 × 2π rad = 7.85 rad. The starting position does not matter, because Δθ = θ − θ₀ is a change in angular position.
questions.working: Net rotation = +1.50 rev − 0.250 rev = +1.25 rev. Δθ = (1.25 rev)(2π rad/rev) = +7.85 rad. θ₀ does not enter, because Δθ = θ − θ₀ is a change. (Total angle turned: 1.75 rev = 11.0 rad. Final angular position: 0.400 rad + 7.85 rad = 8.25 rad. Whole revolution dropped: 0.25 rev = 1.57 rad.)

questions.q: A rigid disk speeds up as it turns about a fixed axle. Point A on the disk is near its rim and point B is near the axle. Which quantity is greater for A than for B?
options: The point's angular velocity about the axle
The point's angular acceleration about the axle
The point's time to make one full turn
The point's speed along its circular path
optionWhy: A student who thinks points farther from the axle rotate faster picks this. Every point of a rigid disk turns through the same angle in the same time, so A and B have the same angular velocity.
A student who identifies angular acceleration with tangential acceleration picks this. A's tangential acceleration, rα, is greater than B's, but both points share the disk's angular acceleration α.
A student who thinks all points move at the same speed picks this: A's longer path would then take longer. All points complete a turn together, because they share one angular velocity.
Both points share the disk's angular velocity, and v = rω, so A, being farther from the axle, moves faster along its path.
questions.explain: Both points share the disk's angular velocity, and v = rω, so A, being farther from the axle, moves faster along its path.

questions.q: A light string is wrapped around a drum of radius R that turns on a fixed axle. Starting from rest, the drum turns with constant angular acceleration α, and the string unwinds without slipping. What length of string unwinds in time t?
options: αt²/2
Rαt²/2
Rαt
Rαt²
optionWhy: A student who takes the angle turned as the length of string picks this. (1/2)αt² is an angle in radians; the length unwound is R times that angle.
The drum turns through Δθ = (1/2)αt² from rest, and the string unwinds the arc length at the rim, Δs = RΔθ = Rαt²/2.
A student who gives the speed of the rim at time t picks this. Rαt is the rate at which string unwinds, in m/s; the length unwound grows as t², not t.
A student who multiplies the final rim speed, Rαt, by the time picks this. The rim speeds up from zero, so its average speed is half the final speed and the length is Rαt²/2.
questions.explain: The drum turns through Δθ = (1/2)αt² from rest, and the string unwinds the arc length at the rim, Δs = RΔθ = Rαt²/2.
questions.working: Angle turned from rest: Δθ = (1/2)αt². The string unwinds the arc length at the rim: Δs = RΔθ = (1/2)Rαt² = Rαt²/2. (Radius left out: αt²/2. Rim speed at time t: Rαt. Final rim speed × t: Rαt².)

questions.q: A merry-go-round speeds up uniformly from 0.50 rad/s to 2.0 rad/s in 5.0 s. What is the tangential acceleration of a point on it 0.60 m from its axis?
optionWhy: A student who takes the angular acceleration as the point's tangential acceleration picks this. α = 0.30 rad/s² must be multiplied by the point's distance from the axis: a_T = rα = 0.18 m/s².
A student who divides the final speed by the time picks this: (0.60 m)(2.0 rad/s)/(5.0 s) = 0.24 m/s². The merry-go-round was already turning at 0.50 rad/s, so only the change in speed counts.
A student who gives the change in the point's speed as its acceleration picks this: (0.60 m)(1.5 rad/s) = 0.90 m/s. That change takes 5.0 s, so the acceleration is (0.90 m/s)/(5.0 s) = 0.18 m/s².
α = Δω/Δt = (2.0 rad/s − 0.50 rad/s)/(5.0 s) = 0.30 rad/s², and a_T = rα = (0.60 m)(0.30 rad/s²) = 0.18 m/s².
questions.explain: α = Δω/Δt = (2.0 rad/s − 0.50 rad/s)/(5.0 s) = 0.30 rad/s², and a_T = rα = (0.60 m)(0.30 rad/s²) = 0.18 m/s².
questions.working: α = Δω/Δt = (2.0 rad/s − 0.50 rad/s)/(5.0 s) = 0.30 rad/s². a_T = rα = (0.60 m)(0.30 rad/s²) = 0.18 m/s². (α itself: 0.30. Final speed/time: (0.60)(2.0)/5.0 = 0.24. Change in speed rΔω: (0.60)(1.5) = 0.90.)

questions.q: A student is drawing a force diagram to analyze the torques exerted on a rigid beam. Which statement about the diagram is correct?
options: It shows the forces that the beam exerts on its supports as well as the forces exerted on it.
It shows each torque exerted on the beam as a curved arrow, drawn in place of the force.
It shows every force exerted on the beam, with each drawn from the beam's center of mass.
It shows only forces that other objects exert on the beam, as a free-body diagram does.
optionWhy: A student who includes both members of each third-law pair picks this. The beam's push on a support is exerted on the support; only forces exerted on the beam belong in its diagram.
A student who thinks torques are separate interactions picks this. The diagram shows the forces; the torque of each force is worked out from where and in what direction the force is exerted.

A student who draws every force from the center of mass, as in a free-body diagram for an object, picks this. For torques the point where each force is exerted matters, so contact forces are drawn where the contact is.

A force diagram is like a free-body diagram: it shows only forces exerted on the chosen system by other objects. Unlike a free-body diagram for an object, it also shows where on the beam each force is exerted, so that torques can be found.
questions.explain: A force diagram is like a free-body diagram: it shows only forces exerted on the chosen system by other objects. Unlike a free-body diagram for an object, it also shows where on the beam each force is exerted, so that torques can be found.

questions.q: The torque exerted by a force about an axis is τ⃗ = r⃗ × F⃗. Which describes the direction of τ⃗?
options: At right angles to the plane that contains both r⃗ and F⃗
Along F⃗, in the direction in which the force pushes or pulls
In the plane of r⃗ and F⃗, pointing between the two vectors
Along the path of the point where the force is exerted
optionWhy: A cross product is perpendicular to both of its vectors, so τ⃗ is perpendicular to the plane that contains r⃗ and F⃗: along the axis about which the force tends to turn the system. The right-hand rule picks which of the two perpendicular directions.
A student who gives a torque the direction of the force that produces it picks this. τ⃗ = r⃗ × F⃗ is perpendicular to F⃗, so a nonzero torque is never along it.
A student who treats the cross product like a vector sum picks this. A sum of two vectors lies in their plane; a cross product is perpendicular to that plane.

A student who takes the direction in which the point of application moves as the torque's direction picks this. That point moves tangent to its circle, in the plane of rotation; τ⃗ is perpendicular to that plane.
questions.explain: A cross product is perpendicular to both of its vectors, so τ⃗ is perpendicular to the plane that contains r⃗ and F⃗: along the axis about which the force tends to turn the system. The right-hand rule picks which of the two perpendicular directions.

questions.q: The figure shows a wrench on a bolt at O, seen from above, and a force exerted on the wrench in the plane of the page. What is the magnitude of the torque exerted by the force about O? Use sin 37° = 3/5 and cos 37° = 4/5.
optionWhy: A student who multiplies the whole force by its distance from O picks this: (0.400 m)(20.0 N). The force is not perpendicular to the wrench, and its component along the wrench produces no torque.
Only the component of the force perpendicular to the wrench produces torque: F sin 37° = (20.0 N)(3/5) = 12.0 N, exerted 0.400 m from O. τ = (0.400 m)(12.0 N) = 4.80 N·m.
A student who uses cos 37° picks this: (0.400 m)(20.0 N)(4/5). F cos 37° is the component along the wrench, whose line of action passes through O; the perpendicular component is F sin 37°.
A student who uses the full length of the wrench, 0.500 m, picks this. The force is exerted 0.400 m from O, so that is the distance to use.
questions.explain: Only the component of the force perpendicular to the wrench produces torque: F sin 37° = (20.0 N)(3/5) = 12.0 N, exerted 0.400 m from O. τ = (0.400 m)(12.0 N) = 4.80 N·m.
questions.working: Only the component of F perpendicular to the wrench (and so to r⃗) produces torque: F sin 37° = (20.0 N)(3/5) = 12.0 N, exerted 0.400 m from O. τ = (0.400 m)(12.0 N) = 4.80 N·m. (Whole force: 8.00 N·m. cos 37°: 6.40 N·m. Full length 0.500 m: 6.00 N·m.)

questions.q: A student is asked to describe the rotational inertia of a rigid system about a fixed axis. Which description is correct?
options: How rapidly it is rotating, so it grows as the system's angular velocity about the axis grows
The torque needed to keep the system turning at a steady angular velocity about that axis
Its total mass, which resists rotation equally wherever on the system the mass sits
Its resistance to changes in angular velocity, set by its mass and how far that mass is from the axis
optionWhy: A student who thinks rotational inertia measures how fast a system spins picks this. How fast it rotates is the angular velocity; rotational inertia measures resistance to a change in angular velocity and, for a rigid system, does not depend on it.

A student who thinks rotation needs a continual torque to keep going picks this. Rotational inertia measures a system's resistance to changes in its rotation, not a torque that keeps it turning, and it has units of kg·m², not the N·m of a torque.
A student who thinks rotational inertia depends only on mass picks this. The same mass placed farther from the axis gives a greater rotational inertia, so where the mass is matters.

Rotational inertia is the rotational counterpart of mass as a measure of inertia: the greater it is, the harder it is to start, stop, speed up or slow down the rotation about that axis. It depends on the amount of mass and on its distances from the axis, I = ∫ r² dm.
questions.explain: Rotational inertia is the rotational counterpart of mass as a measure of inertia: the greater it is, the harder it is to start, stop, speed up or slow down the rotation about that axis. It depends on the amount of mass and on its distances from the axis, I = ∫ r² dm.

questions.q: Two thin rods, X and Y, have the same mass and length. In rod X most of the mass is concentrated equally near the two ends; in rod Y most of the mass is concentrated near the middle. Each rod can rotate about an axis through its midpoint, perpendicular to the rod. Which claim about the rods' rotational inertias about these axes is correct?
options: Rod X's is greater, because more of its mass is far from the axis
Rod Y's is greater, because rod X's end masses give it more leverage
They are equal, because the rods have the same mass and length
It depends on where each rod is pushed, not on the rods alone
optionWhy: Each bit of mass contributes r² dm, so mass far from the axis contributes much more than mass near it. Rod X has most of its mass near the ends, far from the midpoint axis, so its rotational inertia is greater.

A student who thinks mass far from the axis is easier to turn, as a force far from the axis gives more torque, picks this. Mass far from the axis increases the rotational inertia, so rod X is the harder one to set rotating.
A student who thinks rotational inertia is set by mass (and size) alone picks this. The distribution of the mass also matters, and the two rods distribute their equal masses differently.

A student who mixes up torque and rotational inertia picks this. Where a rod is pushed affects the torque on it, not its rotational inertia, which depends only on its mass and the mass's distances from the axis.
questions.explain: Each bit of mass contributes r² dm, so mass far from the axis contributes much more than mass near it. Rod X has most of its mass near the ends, far from the midpoint axis, so its rotational inertia is greater.

questions.q: An irregularly shaped flat plate can rotate about either of two axes perpendicular to its face. Axis 1 and axis 2 are each a distance d from the plate's center of mass, on opposite sides of it, and axis 1 is nearer the heavier part of the plate. Which claim about the plate's rotational inertias about the two axes, I₁ and I₂, is correct?
options: I₁ < I₂, because axis 1 is nearer the plate's heavier part
I₁ = I₂, as both axes are equally far from the center of mass
I₁ > I₂, as the heavy part near axis 1 has less leverage
They cannot be compared, as the plate is not symmetric
optionWhy: A student who expects a smaller rotational inertia when the axis is near the heavy part picks this. The mass distribution is already accounted for in the position of the center of mass; equal d gives equal I.

Both axes are parallel to the axis through the center of mass and a distance d from it, so the parallel axis theorem gives each I_cm + Md². The theorem holds for any rigid object, so the plate's irregular shape does not matter.

A student who thinks mass far from an axis is easier to turn, by leverage, concludes that the plate is harder to turn about axis 1. Mass far from the axis increases I, and here the parallel axis theorem gives equal values.
A student who thinks the parallel axis theorem needs a symmetric object picks this. The theorem follows from the definition of the center of mass and holds for any rigid system.
questions.explain: Both axes are parallel to the axis through the center of mass and a distance d from it, so the parallel axis theorem gives each I_cm + Md². The theorem holds for any rigid object, so the plate's irregular shape does not matter.

questions.q: The graph shows the angular velocity of a wheel as a function of time. During which time intervals is the net torque exerted on the wheel not zero?
options: From 0 s to 7 s, the whole time that the wheel is turning
From 0 s to 5 s, up until the wheel begins to slow
From 0 s to 2 s, while the wheel is speeding up
From 0 s to 2 s and from 5 s to 7 s, while ω changes
optionWhy: A student who thinks a turning wheel needs a net torque that grows with its angular velocity picks this. From 2 s to 5 s ω is constant, so the net torque is zero even though the wheel is turning fastest.

A student who thinks a net torque is needed to keep the wheel turning, and that the wheel slows once that torque stops, picks this. From 2 s to 5 s ω is constant, so the net torque is zero; from 5 s to 7 s ω decreases, which requires a net torque opposite to the rotation.
A student who thinks a wheel slows down on its own picks only the speeding-up interval. From 5 to 7 s ω decreases, which also requires a net torque, opposite to the rotation.

If the torques on a rigid system are not balanced, its angular velocity must be changing, and if ω is constant the net torque is zero. ω changes (nonzero slope) from 0 to 2 s and from 5 to 7 s, so those are the intervals with a nonzero net torque.
questions.explain: If the torques on a rigid system are not balanced, its angular velocity must be changing, and if ω is constant the net torque is zero. ω changes (nonzero slope) from 0 to 2 s and from 5 to 7 s, so those are the intervals with a nonzero net torque.
questions.working: Net torque is nonzero exactly when ω is changing, where the graph's slope is not zero: from 0 to 2 s (increasing) and from 5 to 7 s (decreasing).

questions.q: A uniform disk rests on a horizontal frictionless surface. The diagram shows the two horizontal forces then exerted on it, of equal magnitude, at opposite points on its edge. Which claim about the disk's subsequent motion is correct?
options: It starts rotating, while its center of mass stays at rest
It starts rotating, and its center of mass accelerates to the right
Its center of mass accelerates to the right; it does not rotate
It moves to the right at a constant velocity, and it does not rotate
optionWhy: A student who thinks forces exerted at the edge produce rotation instead of translation picks this. Every external force contributes to a_cm, here 2F/M to the right, and the two torques cancel, so the disk does not rotate.

A student who thinks each off-center force makes the disk rotate on its own picks this. The top force tends to turn the disk clockwise and the bottom force counterclockwise, with equal torques, so the net torque is zero.

The forces add to 2F to the right, so the center of mass accelerates. Their torques about the center are equal in magnitude, FR, and opposite in sense, so the net torque is zero and the disk's angular velocity stays zero: it is in rotational equilibrium but not translational equilibrium.
A student who thinks a constant net force produces a constant velocity picks this. The net force is 2F, so the center of mass accelerates; its velocity does not stay constant.
questions.explain: The forces add to 2F to the right, so the center of mass accelerates. Their torques about the center are equal in magnitude, FR, and opposite in sense, so the net torque is zero and the disk's angular velocity stays zero: it is in rotational equilibrium but not translational equilibrium.
questions.working: Net force = 2F to the right, so the center of mass accelerates (a_cm = 2F/M). About the center, the top force's torque is clockwise and the bottom force's is counterclockwise, each of magnitude FR, so the net torque is zero and ω stays zero.

questions.q: A rod of mass M lies at rest on a horizontal frictionless surface. A small thruster fixed to one end of the rod then exerts on it a force of constant magnitude F, always parallel to the surface and perpendicular to the rod. Which claim about the rod's motion while the thruster acts is correct?
options: Its center of mass accelerates at less than F/M, as it starts rotating
Its center of mass accelerates at F/M, and its rotation speeds up
Its center of mass stays at rest, and it starts rotating about its center
Its center of mass accelerates at F/M, and it turns at a steady rate
optionWhy: A student who thinks part of the force is used up in rotation picks this. The center-of-mass acceleration is F_net/M = F/M whatever point the force acts at; the rotation does not reduce it.

The center of mass responds to the net external force, wherever it acts: a_cm = F/M in magnitude. Separately, F has a lever arm of half the rod's length about the center of mass, so the net torque is constant and not zero, and the angular velocity keeps increasing. The two analyses are independent.
A student who pictures the rod pivoting about its center, as if on an axle, picks this. No axle holds the rod, so the net force F accelerates its center of mass.
A student who thinks a constant torque produces a constant angular velocity picks this. A constant net torque produces a constant angular acceleration, so the rod's rotation keeps speeding up.
questions.explain: The center of mass responds to the net external force, wherever it acts: a_cm = F/M in magnitude. Separately, F has a lever arm of half the rod's length about the center of mass, so the net torque is constant and not zero, and the angular velocity keeps increasing. The two analyses are independent.

questions.q: A merry-go-round is given a push and then left to turn on its own. A student observes that it slows down steadily and claims that a nonzero net torque is being exerted on it. Which reasoning correctly supports the claim?
options: The push left a torque in its direction of rotation that is still acting, though it is weakening
Its angular velocity is changing, which happens only when the torques on it are unbalanced
It is still rotating, and any rotating object must have a net torque exerted on it to keep turning
Friction acts on it, and any force exerted on a rotating object produces a torque on it
optionWhy: A student who thinks the push leaves a torque behind that gradually dies away picks this. Once the push ends, no torque in the direction of rotation remains; the net torque that is acting is opposite to the rotation.

Angular velocity changes when, and only when, the net torque on a rigid system is not zero. The merry-go-round's angular velocity is decreasing, so a net torque, opposite to its rotation, must be acting (here, friction at the axle and air resistance).

A student who thinks rotation itself requires a net torque picks this. A merry-go-round turning at constant angular velocity would have zero net torque; the evidence for a net torque is that ω is changing.

A student who thinks every force produces a torque, whatever its lever arm, picks this. A force whose line of action passes through the axis exerts no torque, so the existence of a force alone does not establish a net torque.
questions.explain: Angular velocity changes when, and only when, the net torque on a rigid system is not zero. The merry-go-round's angular velocity is decreasing, so a net torque, opposite to its rotation, must be acting (here, friction at the axle and air resistance).

questions.q: A mechanic pushes on a wrench, exerting a constant torque of 40 N·m on a rusted bolt for 5.0 s, but the bolt does not turn. Which statement about the energy the torque transfers to the bolt, with its reasoning, is correct?
options: Some energy, as the torque was exerted on the bolt for a time interval of 5.0 s.
None, as the rust exerts an equal and opposite torque that balances it.
None, as the bolt turned through no angle while the torque was exerted on it.
None, as the bolt's angular speed did not change during the 5.0 s.
optionWhy: A student who links the energy a torque transfers to how long it acts picks this. Work depends on the angular displacement, not the time: with no rotation the work is exactly zero, however long the torque acts.

A student who confuses the work done by one torque with the net work picks this. A balanced torque does work whenever the object turns, as a motor's torque does on a wheel turning steadily against friction; here it does none only because the bolt does not turn.
The work done by a torque is W = ∫τ dθ. The bolt did not rotate, so Δθ = 0 and the torque, however large and however long it is exerted, did no work on the bolt.

A student who thinks energy is transferred only when speed changes picks this. A motor turning a wheel at constant speed against friction transfers energy to it; what makes the work zero here is the zero angular displacement.
questions.explain: The work done by a torque is W = ∫τ dθ. The bolt did not rotate, so Δθ = 0 and the torque, however large and however long it is exerted, did no work on the bolt.
questions.working: W = ∫τ dθ = (40 N·m)(0 rad) = 0 J: no angular displacement, so no work, independent of the 5.0 s duration.

questions.q: A rope wound around a winch drum of radius 0.20 m is pulled with a constant force of magnitude 50 N, tangent to the drum, while the drum turns through 3.0 revolutions. How much work does the torque exerted by the rope do on the drum?
optionWhy: The torque is τ = rF = (0.20 m)(50 N) = 10 N·m, and the angular displacement is 3.0 rev × 2π rad/rev = 6.0π rad ≈ 18.8 rad. W = τΔθ = (10 N·m)(18.8 rad) ≈ 1.9 × 10² J. As a check, this equals the force times the length of rope pulled off, (50 N)(2π × 0.20 m × 3.0).
A student who uses the number of revolutions as the angular displacement picks this: (10 N·m)(3.0) = 30 J. W = τΔθ needs Δθ in radians, and 3.0 rev is 6.0π rad.
A student who leaves the lever arm out of the torque picks this: (50 N)(6.0π rad) ≈ 940 J. The torque of the rope is rF = 10 N·m, not 50 N·m.
A student who takes the torque itself, 10 N·m, as the energy transferred picks this. Torque and work share the unit N·m, but the work is the torque multiplied by the angular displacement, 6.0π rad.
questions.explain: The torque is τ = rF = (0.20 m)(50 N) = 10 N·m, and the angular displacement is 3.0 rev × 2π rad/rev = 6.0π rad ≈ 18.8 rad. W = τΔθ = (10 N·m)(18.8 rad) ≈ 1.9 × 10² J. As a check, this equals the force times the length of rope pulled off, (50 N)(2π × 0.20 m × 3.0).

questions.q: The diagram shows a wheel rotating counterclockwise on a fixed axle. For a short time interval, while the wheel is still rotating counterclockwise, a force F⃗ tangent to the rim is exerted on the wheel at the point shown. Which describes the angular impulse about the axle that this force delivers to the wheel?
options: Counterclockwise, the same sense as the wheel's rotation during the interval
It has no sense, as an angular impulse has a size but no direction
To the right, along the force, like the linear impulse of the force
Clockwise, the same sense as the torque the force exerts about the axle
optionWhy: A student who thinks an impulse acts in the direction of the motion picks this. The angular impulse has the sense of the torque, which is clockwise here; it opposes the rotation and slows the wheel.
A student who treats angular impulse as a plain amount picks this. Angular impulse has the direction of the torque that delivers it; here it is clockwise.
A student who carries over the direction rule for linear impulse picks this. The force's linear impulse is to the right, but its angular impulse about the axle has the sense of its torque: clockwise.

At the top of the rim, a force to the right turns the wheel clockwise about the axle, so its torque is clockwise. Angular impulse has the direction of the torque that delivers it, so it is clockwise, opposite to the wheel's rotation, and it reduces the wheel's angular momentum.
questions.explain: At the top of the rim, a force to the right turns the wheel clockwise about the axle, so its torque is clockwise. Angular impulse has the direction of the torque that delivers it, so it is clockwise, opposite to the wheel's rotation, and it reduces the wheel's angular momentum.

questions.q: Two identical wheels, A and B, are at rest on fixed, frictionless axles. A net torque of 8.0 N·m is exerted on wheel A for 0.50 s, and a net torque of 2.0 N·m is exerted on wheel B for 2.0 s. How do the wheels' angular momenta compare after the torques have ended?
options: Wheel A's is greater, as the torque on wheel A is greater
Wheel B's is greater, as the torque on wheel B acts for longer
Equal, as the two wheels receive equal angular impulses
Equal only if the two wheels turn through equal angles
optionWhy: A student who judges the effect by the size of the torque alone picks this. The torque on B is smaller but acts four times as long, so the angular impulses, and the changes in angular momentum, are equal.
A student who judges the effect by the duration alone picks this. The torque on A acts for a quarter of the time but is four times as large, so the angular impulses are equal.

Each wheel receives an angular impulse τΔt = 4.0 N·m·s (8.0 × 0.50 and 2.0 × 2.0). The angular impulse equals the change in angular momentum, and both wheels start from rest, so they end with equal angular momenta.
A student who links the change in angular momentum to the angle turned, as for work, picks this. The angular impulse is ∫τ dt over time; it does not depend on the angle through which the wheel turns.
questions.explain: Each wheel receives an angular impulse τΔt = 4.0 N·m·s (8.0 × 0.50 and 2.0 × 2.0). The angular impulse equals the change in angular momentum, and both wheels start from rest, so they end with equal angular momenta.
questions.working: A: (8.0 N·m)(0.50 s) = 4.0 N·m·s. B: (2.0 N·m)(2.0 s) = 4.0 N·m·s. ΔL equal; both start from rest, so L_A = L_B.
